clue.text: Book illustrations of some Wedgwood pieces

definitions.meaning: full-page pictures printed separately in a book are called this
dishes of Wedgwood china, flat items for serving food

explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both full-page printed pictures in a volume and flat china dishes such as Wedgwood makes.

clue.text: It is heard in Leeds and seen in Skipton centre

definitions.meaning: Leeds hosts a famous international competition for this keyboard instrument
the middle letter of Skipton is P, the musical abbreviation for soft playing

explanation.surface: Something both audible in one Yorkshire city and visible in another Yorkshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Leeds and Skipton are towns in Yorkshire; the Leeds International Piano Competition is world-famous. The centre letter of SKIPTON is P, which in a score means play softly.
explanation.definitionFit: The instrument is played at the Leeds competition, and as a musical direction meaning soft it is abbreviated to the letter P.

clue.text: Spirit-producing light-rubber

parts.note: the pantomime hero who polished an old lamp and summoned a genie

explanation.definitionFit: In the tale, rubbing the magic lamp (a light) makes the genie (a spirit) appear.

clue.text: Space for deployment of arms

parts.note: reads as military room for weapons, but means space to stretch your arms out

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means enough room to move freely, literally room to stick your elbows out.

clue.text: Going off, chased by police

indicators.note: being chased means the police come after, so their letters follow

parts.note: to go off at speed, to flee, is to have run
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, British detectives

explanation.surface: A fleeing suspect sprinting away with officers in hot pursuit.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a whole the clue also describes food going off; CID is the UK police's detective branch.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that is going off has turned sour and smells bad.

clue.text: A Shaw play — "At the Mercy of the Waves *

definitions.text: At the Mercy of the Waves

indicators.note: the letters of 'A Shaw' play about, moving into a new order

explanation.surface: A drama by George Bernard Shaw with a seafaring title.
explanation.walkthrough: 'play' looks like a noun for a Shaw drama, but it tells you to rearrange A SHAW.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship swamped and tossed by the sea is flooded with water.

clue.text: Sucrose extract for the man who has everything?

indicators.note: an extract is something drawn out and reworked, so the sugar's letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Getting a sugar extract as a gift for someone who already owns it all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extract' looks like a noun but signals that the letters of SUCROSE be rearranged. The king of Lydia was proverbially rich.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Lydian king was so wealthy that his name stands for a person of limitless riches.

clue.text: eg Black Bess — one with unexpected ability

definitions.meaning: Dick Turpin's famous mare, literally a black steed
a contender whose talent was not known beforehand

explanation.surface: A highwayman's mare turning out to be a surprising talent.
explanation.walkthrough: Black Bess was the horse of the English highwayman Dick Turpin.
explanation.definitionFit: Black Bess was a black-coated mount, and the idiom describes an outsider whose skill surprises everyone.

clue.text: Don's expression of surprise makes one cram a BA, desperately

indicators.note: acting desperately suggests frantic disorder, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: An academic exclaims at a student frantically swotting for a degree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Don' looks like a university lecturer but is a Spanish gentleman; 'desperately' rearranges CRAM A BA.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a Spanish exclamation of astonishment, as a Spanish gentleman might say.

clue.text: Chooses to wear rosettes, ribbons, etc

definitions.meaning: to prefer or side with something
badges worn to show support for a team or party

explanation.surface: Picking which ribbons and rosettes to sport at a show.
explanation.definitionFit: To prefer is to show partiality, and supporters' badges and ribbons are tokens of that partiality.

clue.text: Metal of old pennies?

parts.note: a pewter-like alloy shares its name with the seated figure on pre-decimal British coins

explanation.definitionFit: It is the name of a tin-based alloy and of the national emblem stamped on old British pennies.

clue.text: Poet giving value to the things we say

parts.note: what we speak is made of words
worth means value

explanation.surface: A poet who gives weight to everyday speech.
explanation.walkthrough: The value given to words is their worth, read in that order.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lake District writer of 'Daffodils' is one of England's best-known Romantic versifiers.

clue.text: 26'scall in London

definitions.meaning: the printed 26 should read 16, the huntsman, whose cry on sighting a hare this is
a district of the West End

explanation.surface: A hunter's cry heard somewhere in London.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed '26' should be 16, which is HUNTSMAN, and the space after the apostrophe is lost. The West End district took its name from the old hunting cry.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a traditional hunting halloo and the name of a lively West End district in the capital.

clue.text: Whodunnit? Brown — Can't be!

parts.note: dun is a dull greyish-brown
no is a flat refusal

explanation.surface: A reader of a detective story guessing it was Father Brown, and being told otherwise.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the question 'Who did it?', answered with a shrug; Father Brown is a fictional priest-detective.
explanation.definitionFit: The colloquial reply to 'who did it?' when one has no idea is 'I don't know'.

clue.text: Piece of chicken for battering

definitions.meaning: the lower leg of a fowl
a stick used for beating a percussion instrument

explanation.surface: A portion of chicken about to be coated in batter.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a fowl's lower leg and the stick a percussionist beats with.

clue.text: A nuisance in attempt to find Arras

indicators.note: the nuisance phrase goes inside the word for attempt

parts.note: a try is an attempt
a pest is a nuisance

explanation.surface: Something annoying gets in the way of a search for a French town.
explanation.walkthrough: Arras looks like the town in northern France, but an arras is a wall hanging, named after it.
explanation.definitionFit: An arras is a woven wall hanging, a kind of woven picture in cloth.

clue.text: Small change — step into yacht at sea

indicators.note: something at sea is confused, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Advice for boarding a boat on the water, plus some spare coins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' rearranges STEP and YACHT together.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the small float of cash an office keeps for minor expenses.

clue.text: eg Peel — rider in Cambridgeshire now?

definitions.meaning: John Peel was a famous Cumbrian master of foxhounds
a man from Hunts, the old county of Huntingdonshire now absorbed into Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: A rider named Peel out in the Cambridgeshire countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: John Peel is the hunter of the song 'D'ye ken John Peel'. Huntingdonshire (Hunts) was merged into Cambridgeshire in 1974, so a man of Hunts lives there now.
explanation.definitionFit: John Peel led a pack of hounds, and a resident of Hunts is a Hunts man.

clue.text: Roofer got about twopence once — small fry

indicators.note: the roofer's word surrounds the coins, as if getting round them

parts.note: a tiler lays roof tiles
d was the symbol for a penny before decimal coinage, so two of them are DD

explanation.surface: A roofer earning a pittance in old money for little fish.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971 British pennies were written d, so twopence was 2d.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny fish such as a minnow, or by extension an unimportant person.

clue.text: Story about black-board

indicators.note: the story's word goes around the single letter

parts.note: a tale is a story
B is the standard abbreviation for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A tale told about the blackboard in a classroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'black-board' looks like one word but splits: 'black' gives B, and 'board' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Board is an old word for a dining surface, as in bed and board.

clue.text: That of Raleigh was framed

parts.note: Millais's painting of young Walter Raleigh listening to a sailor hangs in a frame

explanation.definitionFit: Millais painted 'The Boyhood of Raleigh', so the explorer's youth was literally put in a frame.

clue.text: Inner house-dog pressed into service

indicators.note: the inner letters of the phrase supply the run

explanation.surface: A dog kept indoors being put to work.
explanation.definitionFit: Something pressed into service has been employed, put to work.

clue.text: Tolkien's vehicle of 19?

parts.note: a child's small bicycle, pictured as transport for the elvish folk Tolkien wrote about, ridden in youth

explanation.walkthrough: 19 is BOYHOOD: the small bicycle of childhood, here imagined as one for Tolkien's elfin creatures.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the old name for a child's small bicycle, and Tolkien wrote of elfin beings.

clue.text: Box in air-trip left out

indicators.note: left out means the letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: a flight is a trip by air

explanation.surface: A box packed for a plane journey is left behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' looks like a container, but means to spar; 'out' drops L from FLIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: To box is to spar with fists, to brawl.

clue.text: Vigorous, powerful drive at Turnberry's last

parts.note: lust is a strong urge or desire

indicators.note: the final letter of the golf course's name is taken

explanation.surface: A golfer hits a long drive at the Turnberry course.
explanation.walkthrough: Turnberry is a famous Scottish golf links, so 'drive' looks like a tee shot.
explanation.definitionFit: Lusty means strong and full of energy, hearty.

clue.text: Life-study of oil-change in bad spirit

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go inside the spirit

parts.note: a bogy is an evil spirit or goblin

indicators.note: the letters of the word change their order

explanation.surface: Studying how an oil change goes when you are in a bad mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad spirit' looks like a mood, but a bogy is a goblin; 'change' and 'in' are the two indicators.
explanation.definitionFit: The science concerned with living organisms is literally the study of life.

clue.text: Leave quickly — it is the Virginia elk!

parts.note: VA is the US postal abbreviation for Virginia
the elk of Europe is called a moose in America

explanation.surface: Shouted at an American elk to make it run off.
explanation.walkthrough: In North America the animal the British call an elk is a moose.
explanation.definitionFit: It is American slang for clearing off fast, from Spanish 'vamos'.

clue.text: Serving chops the oriental way?

parts.note: reads as dishing up cuts of meat in Asian style, but means delivering hand blows in a Japanese fighting art

explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese martial art is famous for its chopping hand strikes.

clue.text: Timid about left over wool-waste

indicators.note: the word for timid goes around the other piece

parts.note: shy means timid
an odd item is one left over, unmatched

explanation.surface: A nervous person dealing with leftover scraps of wool.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoddy is cloth made from recycled scraps of woollen fibre.
